text: A Random Neural Network neuron stores a non-negative integer potential k and receives excitatory (+1) and inhibitory (−1) spikes that arrive as independent Poisson processes.
source_span: Stochastic “spiking” neuron that stores an *integer* “potential” \(k\ge 0\). It receives **excitatory** (+1) and **inhibitory** (‑1) spikes that arrive as independent Poisson processes.

text: The steady-state firing probability in Random Neural Networks has a closed-form product-form solution.
source_span: The steady‑state firing probability has a **closed‑form product‑form** solution.

text: In Random Neural Networks the probability that a neuron is excited evolves according to a birth-death process (Markovian).
source_span: Markovian: the probability that a neuron is “excited” (i.e., \(k>0\)) evolves according to a birth‑death process.

text: Random Neural Network outputs can be interpreted as firing probabilities in [0,1] that can be used directly as class-posteriors.
source_span: Firing probability of output neurons, i.e. the steady‑state probability they are excited. This value lives in \([0,1]\) and can be interpreted directly as a class‑posterior.

text: Weights in Random Neural Networks represent rates or probabilities at which a neuron sends excitatory or inhibitory spikes to another neuron, often written as p_ij^+ or p_ij^- with sum_j (p_ij^+ + p_ij^-) ≤ 1.
source_span: Rate at which neuron \(i\) sends *excitatory* (or inhibitory) spikes to neuron \(j\). Often written as \(p_{ij}^{+}\) for excitatory probability or \(p_{ij}^{-}\) for inhibitory probability, with \(\sum_{j} (p_{ij}^{+}+p_{ij}^{-}) \le 1\).

text: In Random Neural Networks inhibition is modeled explicitly via separate excitatory and inhibitory channels rather than as negative weights.
source_span: Separate excitatory / inhibitory channels; there is no “negative weight” per se— inhibition is modeled explicitly.

text: Because of the product-form solution, deep recurrent random neural networks can be trained without unrolling or back-propagation through time.
source_span: Because of the product‑form solution, *any* directed graph that respects the “routing probability” constraints also enjoys an analytically tractable steady state. Hence, deep recurrent random neural networks can be trained without unrolling or back‑propagation through time.

text: The steady-state firing probability π_i satisfies the equation π_i = (λ_i + Σ_j r_j p_{ji}^+ π_j) / (r_i + Σ_j r_j p_{ji}^- π_j).
source_span: Because the steady‑state firing probability \(\pi_i\) satisfies a **linear equation**: \(\pi_i = \frac{\lambda_i + \sum_{j} r_j p_{ji}^{+}\pi_j}{r_i + \sum_{j} r_j p_{ji}^{-}\pi_j}\).

text: When you train a machine learning model on bulk or single‑cell gene‑expression data that comes from many different tissue types, the model can easily learn tissue‑of‑origin signatures instead of cancer‑specific signals.
source_span: When you train a machine learning (ML) model on bulk or single‑cell gene‑expression data that comes from many different tissue types, the model can easily “cheat” by learning **tissue‑of‑origin (ToO) signatures** instead of the cancer‑specific signals you really care about.

text: If tissue signatures are not accounted for, a putative biomarker can appear cancer‑specific simply because the training set contained more tumor samples from one tissue and more normal samples from another.
source_span: If these tissue signatures are not accounted for, any putative biomarker will be confounded: it will look “cancer‑specific” simply because the training set happened to contain more tumor samples from tissue A and more normal samples from tissue B, etc.

text: Feeding the model the tissue label or a low‑dimensional embedding of it allows the model to condition its predictions on tissue.
source_span: By feeding the model the tissue label (or a low‑dimensional embedding of it) you give it a chance to *condition* its predictions on tissue, rather than using tissue as a hidden proxy.

text: One‑hot encoding tissue labels and concatenating them to gene expression features is a valid approach for linear models.
source_span:
One‑hot encode tissue and concatenate with expression data

X_aug = np.hstack([X, T])   # now has n_genes + n_tissues‑1 columns

text: A tissue embedding concatenated to a hidden representation can be used in deep learning models to condition predictions on tissue.
source_span: Add a *conditional* batch‑normalization layer or a *tissue embedding* that is concatenated to the hidden representation before the final classifier.

text: Performing a stratified split by both class (tumor vs normal) and tissue ensures each tissue appears in both folds.
source_span: - **Train‑test split**: Perform a *stratified* split **by both class (tumor vs normal) and tissue** so that each tissue appears in both folds.

text: Using GroupKFold with tissue as the group forces the model to generalize across tissues during cross‑validation.
source_span: - **Cross‑validation**: Use *group‑k‑fold* where each group is a tissue type (`sklearn.model_selection.GroupKFold`). This forces the model to generalize across tissues, not just memorize them.

text: Fitting a linear model of expression ~ tissue within the normal samples and subtracting the fitted tissue component from all samples is a residualization strategy.
source_span: Fit a linear model of expression ~ tissue (one‑hot encoded) **within the normal samples only**, then subtract the fitted tissue component from *all* samples (tumor + normal).

text: Most academic consortia, biotech programs, and regulatory‑grade biomarker projects follow a multistage pipeline from in‑silico discovery to real‑world clinical implementation today (2023‑2026).

text: Inside a cold, isolated neutron star the temperature is low enough that the EOS is effectively a one-parameter relation P(ρ).
source_span: Inside a cold, isolated neutron star (NS) the temperature is low enough that the EOS is effectively a **one‑parameter** relation \(P(ho)\).

text: A static, spherically symmetric star in hydrostatic equilibrium obeys the Tolman‑Oppenheimer‑Volkoff (TOV) equations.
source_span: General relativity tells us that a static, spherically symmetric star in hydrostatic equilibrium obeys the **Tolman‑Oppenheimer‑Volkoff (TOV) equations**

text: Given an EOS P(ρ), integrating the TOV equations from the centre outward until the pressure drops to zero yields a unique pair (M,R) for that central density.
source_span: Given an EOS \(P(ho)\), we can **integrate the TOV equations** from the centre (\(r=0\), specified central density \(ho_c\)) outward until the pressure drops to zero. The result is a **unique pair \((M,R)\)** for that central density.

text: Varying the central density traces out a mass‑radius (M‑R) curve that is a direct fingerprint of the underlying EOS.
source_span: Varying \(ho_c\) traces out a **mass‑radius (M‑R) curve** that is a direct fingerprint of the underlying EOS.

text: Every admissible EOS predicts a specific M‑R relation.
source_span: * **Every admissible EOS predicts a specific M‑R relation.**

text: Every observed (M,R) point must lie on (or very close to) the curve belonging to the true EOS.
source_span: * **Every observed \\((M,R)\\) point must lie on (or very close to) the curve belonging to the true EOS.**

text: The maximum mass M_max probes the pressure at approximately 5–10 ρ_sat.
source_span: | **Maximum mass \(M_{\max}\)** | Pressure at **~5–10 \( \rho_{\rm sat}\)** (densities reached in the core of the most massive NS) |

text: The radius of a canonical-mass star R_1.4 for M≈1.4 M_sun is sensitive to pressure around 1–2 ρ_sat.
source_span: | **Radius of a canonical‑mass star (\(R_{1.4}\) for \(M\simeq1.4\,M_\odot\))** | Pressure around **\(1–2\,\rho_{\rm sat}\)** (the outer core) |

text: In a one-dimensional non-Hermitian lattice the Bloch Hamiltonian H(k) depends on a single crystal momentum k in [-π,π] and on a set of tunable control parameters λ.
source_span: In a **one‑dimensional (1D) non‑Hermitian lattice** (e.g., a photonic waveguide array, an electronic circuit, a cold‑atom chain with controlled loss, or a mechanical metamaterial) the Bloch Hamiltonian \(H(k)\) depends on a single crystal momentum \(k\in[-\pi,\pi]\) and on a set of **tunable control parameters** \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}=(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\dots )\) that can be varied in time.

text: When parameters are driven along a closed loop C in parameter space the instantaneous eigenstates acquire a non-adiabatic cyclic geometric phase.
source_span: When the parameters are driven along a closed loop \(\mathcal C\) in the \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\)-space, the instantaneous eigenstates \(|\psi_{n}(k;\boldsymbol{\lambda})\rangle\) acquire a **non‑adiabatic cyclic geometric phase** (the non‑Hermitian analogue of the Berry phase).

text: If the loop encircles one or more exceptional points of the band structure the geometric phase is branch-cut dependent and can change by integer multiples of π (or 2π for bi-orthogonal phases) each time the loop winds around an EP.
source_span: If the loop **encircles one or more exceptional points (EPs)** of the band structure, the geometric phase is **branch‑cut dependent** and can change by integer multiples of \(\pi\) (or \(2\pi\) for bi‑orthogonal phases) each time the loop winds around an EP.

text: Detecting the effect experimentally requires a platform in which both the non-Hermitian band structure and the control parameters can be measured with momentum resolution.
source_span: Detecting this effect experimentally requires (i) a platform in which **both the non‑Hermitian band structure and the control parameters can be measured with momentum resolution**, and (ii) a protocol that **extracts the accumulated phase** after a *single* cycle (or after several cycles to resolve winding numbers).

source_span: | **Photonic waveguide arrays** (silica, laser‑written) | Spatially patterned gain/loss or asymmetric evanescent coupling (complex coupling constants) |

text: Fourier-space imaging of the output intensity in photonic waveguides gives the distribution in k, with phase retrieval via interferometry.
source_span: | **Photonic waveguide arrays** ... | **Fourier‑space imaging** of the output intensity gives the distribution in \(k\). Phase retrieval via interferometry.

text: Coupled resonator optical lattices can introduce non-Hermiticity via intrinsic loss, engineered gain, or dissipative coupling via auxiliary waveguides.
source_span: | **Coupled resonator optical lattices** (microring, whispering‑gallery) | Intrinsic loss, engineered gain (optical pumping), or dissipative coupling via auxiliary waveguides |

text: Electrical LC-R circuits can introduce non-Hermiticity via negative resistors (NICs) or balanced gain-loss nodes giving complex admittance.

text: The decay B_{(s)}^{0} -> mu^{+} mu^{-} is one of the cleanest, most suppressed processes in the Standard Model.
source_span: The decay **\(B_{(s)}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\)** is one of the cleanest, most suppressed processes in the Standard Model (SM).

text: Its SM branching fraction is known to better than 10% (theoretical).
source_span: Its SM branching fraction is known to better than 10 % (theoretical)

text: The decay is measured experimentally at the few-×10⁻⁹ level.
source_span: and measured experimentally at the few‑×10⁻⁹ level.

text: The decay proceeds only through higher-order (loop) diagrams in the Standard Model.
source_span: Because the decay proceeds only through higher‑order (loop) diagrams,

text: New heavy particles that can appear in those loops (e.g. supersymmetric particles, extra Z' bosons, lepto-quarks, Higgs-like scalars) will change the effective couplings (Wilson coefficients) that govern the decay.
source_span: any new heavy particle that can appear in those loops—​supersymmetric particles, extra Z′ bosons, lepto‑quarks, Higgs‑like scalars, etc.​— will change the **effective couplings (Wilson coefficients)** that govern the decay.

text: A precise measurement that matches the SM prediction tightens the allowed size of new-physics contributions, translating into lower bounds on the masses or couplings of the extra particles.
source_span: A precise measurement that matches the SM prediction therefore **tightens the allowed size of those new‑physics contributions**, translating into lower bounds on the masses or couplings of the extra particles.

text: If a future measurement deviates significantly from the SM value, it would be a smoking-gun for physics beyond the Standard Model.
source_span: If a future measurement deviates significantly from the SM value, it would be a *smoking‑gun* for physics beyond the SM (BSM).

text: B_{(s)}^{0} -> mu+ mu- is a flavor-changing neutral current (FCNC) forbidden at tree level in the Standard Model and occurs only via loop (penguin & box) diagrams.
source_span: | **Flavor‑changing neutral current (FCNC)** | Forbidden at tree level in the SM → only loop (penguin & box) diagrams.
